section_content.title: Financial Ratios

body.text: **Gross profit margin** = (gross profit / revenue) x 100. It shows how much of every pound of revenue is left after direct production costs (cost of sales). A rising gross margin suggests the firm is managing production costs well or gaining pricing power.

**Operating profit margin** = (operating profit / revenue) x 100. This deducts all operating expenses (rent, wages, marketing) from gross profit, showing the profit from core business operations before interest and tax. It is a better measure of management efficiency than gross margin because it includes overhead control.

**ROCE (Return on Capital Employed)** = (operating profit / capital employed) x 100. Capital employed = total equity + non-current liabilities. ROCE measures how effectively the firm uses its long-term finance to generate profit. It is the single most important ratio for investors comparing alternative investments.

body.result: Context reveals whether performance is genuinely strong or weak

sections.title: Profitability Ratios

the second word of the ratio name

→ A margin that falls while revenue rises points to rising ___

sections.keyIdea: Profitability ratios measure how effectively a firm turns revenue into profit — but a number in isolation means nothing; it must be compared year-on-year, against competitors, or against the industry average.
sections.examMatters: Examiners penalise students who calculate correctly but fail to interpret. Always state what the ratio shows, compare it to a benchmark, and explain what might cause the figure. A ratio tells you what is happening — your job is to explain why.

realExample.text: Apple consistently achieves a gross profit margin of around 45%, compared to Samsung's roughly 35%. This reflects Apple's pricing power — its brand allows premium prices that Samsung's hardware-focused model cannot match, despite Samsung selling more units globally.

sections.misconception: Students calculate a ratio and declare it 'good' or 'bad' with no comparison. Wrong — a 10% operating margin is excellent in grocery retail (Tesco) but poor in luxury goods (LVMH). Instead write: always compare ratios in context — against the firm's own history, its competitors, and the industry average.

body.text: **Current ratio** = current assets / current liabilities. It measures whether the firm can meet its short-term debts. A ratio of 1.5-2.0 is generally healthy — below 1.0 signals potential cash flow crisis, while much above 2.0 suggests idle resources that could be invested.

**Gearing** = (non-current liabilities / capital employed) x 100. It shows what proportion of long-term finance comes from debt rather than equity. High gearing (above 50%) means the firm is heavily reliant on borrowing, which amplifies both profits and losses — a double-edged sword.

High gearing increases **financial risk** because interest must be paid regardless of profit. In good times, debt magnifies returns to shareholders (because they keep all profit after fixed interest payments). In bad times, the fixed interest burden can push the firm towards insolvency. This is the fundamental trade-off of leverage.

body.result: High gearing amplifies losses — the firm may be unable to service its debt

sections.title: Liquidity and Gearing Ratios
sections.keyIdea: A profitable firm can still collapse if it runs out of cash — liquidity ratios check short-term survival, while gearing measures how dependent the firm is on borrowed money and the financial risk that creates.
sections.examMatters: Examiners love to test the limitations of ratios. Always include: ratios show what, not why; they are backward-looking (based on past data); they can be manipulated through accounting choices; and they must be compared in context to have any meaning.

realExample.text: Tesla's ROCE improved dramatically from negative figures in 2019 to over 25% by 2023 as production scaled up and the firm turned consistently profitable. Investors tracked this ratio as proof that Tesla was transitioning from a cash-burning start-up to an efficient manufacturer.

sections.misconception: Students say high gearing is always bad. Wrong — in stable industries with predictable cash flows (utilities, supermarkets), high gearing is manageable because revenue is reliable. Instead write: whether high gearing is risky depends on the stability of the firm's revenue — predictable cash flows can safely support more debt.

takeaway: Gross margin, operating margin, and ROCE measure profitability — ROCE is the most important for investors.
Current ratio checks short-term survival; gearing measures financial risk from borrowing.
Ratios in isolation are meaningless — always compare year-on-year, vs competitors, and vs industry averages.

steps: Compare over time and against competitors

section_notes.title: Financial Ratios for Competitiveness

items.text: Gross profit margin — (gross profit / revenue) × 100; shows the percentage of revenue remaining after direct costs.
Operating profit margin — (operating profit / revenue) × 100; shows profitability after all operating costs, a better indicator of management efficiency.
Return on capital employed (ROCE) — (operating profit / capital employed) × 100; measures how efficiently the firm uses its total capital.
Current ratio — current assets / current liabilities; measures short-term liquidity; ideally 1.5–2.0.
Gearing ratio — (long-term debt / capital employed) × 100; measures the proportion of capital funded by debt; high gearing = high financial risk.
Ratios are most meaningful in context — compare year-on-year (trend), against competitors (benchmarking), or against industry averages.
Ratios tell you what is happening but not why. A falling ROCE could mean falling profits, rising capital employed, or both — you need qualitative analysis too.
Financial ratios link to competitiveness: a firm with higher ROCE and profit margins than rivals has a competitive advantage in attracting investment.

section_notes.keyIdea: Financial ratios convert raw accounting data into comparable metrics that reveal a firm's profitability, liquidity, and efficiency — they are most useful when compared over time or against competitors.
takeaway: Key ratios: profit margins, ROCE, current ratio, gearing.
Always compare: year-on-year, vs competitors, vs industry.
Ratios show what's happening; qualitative analysis explains why.
section_notes.examMatters: Examiners expect accurate calculations, then evaluation. Don't just state the ratio — interpret it: 'ROCE has fallen from 18% to 12%, suggesting the firm's efficiency has deteriorated, possibly due to the £5m investment in new equipment that has not yet generated returns.'
section_notes.misconception: Students think a single ratio tells the full story. Wrong because ratios must be compared in context and combined with qualitative information. Instead write: financial ratios are diagnostic tools — they highlight symptoms, not causes. Always combine ratio analysis with qualitative context from the case study.

section_quiz.question: A firm has revenue of £500,000 and gross profit of £200,000. Its gross profit margin is:
A firm has operating profit of £60,000 and capital employed of £400,000. Its ROCE is:
A firm has current assets of £80,000 and current liabilities of £50,000. Its current ratio is:
A firm has non-current liabilities of £300,000 and capital employed of £500,000. Its gearing ratio is:
section_quiz.explanation: Gearing = (£300,000 ÷ £500,000) × 100 = 60%. This is above 50%, so the firm is highly geared.

section_quiz.question: Which ratio EXCLUDES inventory from the calculation?
section_quiz.explanation: The acid test (quick ratio) = (Current assets − Inventory) ÷ Current liabilities. It excludes inventory because it may not be easily converted to cash.

options: High overhead costs relative to gross profit
section_quiz.question: A firm's high gross profit margin but low net profit margin suggests:
section_quiz.explanation: If gross profit margin is high but net profit margin is low, the gap must be caused by high overheads (rent, salaries, marketing, depreciation) eating into gross profit.

section_quiz.question: Labour turnover is calculated as:
section_quiz.explanation: Labour turnover = (Number of staff leaving ÷ Average number of staff) × 100%. It measures the rate at which employees leave the organisation.

section_quiz.question: Which HR strategy involves giving employees greater authority over their work?
section_quiz.explanation: Empowerment involves delegating authority and responsibility to employees, giving them greater control over their work and decision-making.

options: Manipulating financial figures to present a better picture
section_quiz.question: Window dressing in accounting refers to:
section_quiz.explanation: Window dressing is the practice of manipulating financial data to make the firm's financial position appear more favourable than it actually is.

options: The firm is generating excellent returns
Debt finance is adding value to the firm
The firm is destroying value by using debt finance
The firm should increase its gearing
section_quiz.question: If a firm's ROCE is 8% and its cost of borrowing is 10%, this means:
section_quiz.explanation: If ROCE (8%) is less than the cost of borrowing (10%), the firm earns less on its capital than it pays in interest — debt finance is destroying rather than creating value.

section_practice.guidance: Competitive advantage is a condition that allows a business to outperform its rivals by generating superior value for customers or operating at lower costs (1 mark). It enables the business to earn above-average returns in its industry (1 mark). Example: Apple achieves competitive advantage through product design, innovation and its ecosystem of integrated devices and services (1 mark). This creates high switching costs and strong brand loyalty that competitors find very difficult to replicate (1 mark).
section_practice.question: Define the term 'competitive advantage' and give one example of how a business might achieve it. (4 marks)

section_practice.guidance:
SwiftDeliver currently occupies the low price position (position 2) on Bowman's Strategic Clock (1 mark). Option 1 — move to hybrid (position 3): improve service reliability while keeping prices competitive, offering better value than rivals (1 mark). Option 2 — move to differentiation (position 4): invest heavily in speed and reliability to justify premium prices (1 mark).

Risks: improving service while maintaining low prices may squeeze profit margins (1 mark); moving to higher prices without first proving improved quality could lose existing price-sensitive customers (1 mark). The hybrid strategy is likely more feasible as a first step, gradually building reputation before considering premium pricing (1 mark).
section_practice.question: SwiftDeliver is a parcel delivery company competing primarily on low prices, but losing customers to competitors offering faster, more reliable services at slightly higher prices. Analyse how Bowman's Strategic Clock could help SwiftDeliver reposition itself. (6 marks)

section_practice.guidance: Work from the numbers. A gross margin above the industry average says production and pricing are sound, so the problem lies below gross profit: operating expenses are consuming almost all of it, which points at overheads, marketing or distribution rather than at the product. The current ratio halving to 0.9 says current liabilities now exceed current assets, so the firm may not meet debts falling due. Judgement: profitability and liquidity are telling different stories, and the liquidity trend is the more urgent because a firm can trade profitably and still fail. Evaluate the limits of the comparison — one industry average, two years, no cash flow statement, and no sight of whether the fall in the ratio is a deliberate investment or a loss of control.
section_practice.question: A regional bakery reports a gross profit margin of 42% (industry average 38%) and a profit-for-the-year margin of 3% (industry average 9%). Its current ratio has fallen from 1.8 to 0.9 in two years. Assess what these figures tell the directors about the business. (12 marks)

section_practice.guidance:
Introduction: Define sustainable competitive advantage and its importance in the technology industry (2 marks).

Factor 1 — Innovation and R&D: continuous investment drives differentiation through new features (2 marks), but innovation provides only temporary advantage as competitors quickly imitate (1 mark).

Factor 2 — Brand loyalty and ecosystem: switching costs from an integrated ecosystem of devices, services and software create lasting differentiation (3 marks); this is arguably the strongest source of sustainable advantage in smartphones (1 mark).

Factor 3 — Supply chain efficiency and economies of scale: cost advantages help compete on price, but can be replicated by well-funded competitors (2 marks).

Factor 4 — Intellectual property: patents provide legal protection but expire and can be designed around (2 marks).

Factor 5 — Services revenue and data: recurring revenue from apps, subscriptions and services provides stability beyond hardware sales (2 marks).

Evaluation: The manufacturer's declining share suggests that hardware features alone are insufficient against low-cost competitors. The most sustainable advantage lies in ecosystem lock-in, brand premium and services revenue rather than hardware specifications. Porter would warn against being 'stuck in the middle' — the company must choose between cost leadership and differentiation rather than attempting both. However, no competitive advantage is truly permanent in technology — the key is building multiple reinforcing advantages that are collectively very difficult to replicate (3 marks).
section_practice.question: A leading smartphone manufacturer has seen its global market share decline from 25% to 15% over four years as Chinese competitors offer comparable technology at significantly lower prices. Evaluate the most important factors in maintaining a sustainable competitive advantage in a rapidly changing industry. (20 marks)

section_practice.guidance: Gross profit is revenue less cost of sales: 800,000 less 460,000 is 340,000. Gross profit margin is 340,000 divided by 800,000, times 100, which is 42.5% (2 marks). Profit for the year is gross profit less operating expenses: 340,000 less 260,000 is 80,000. The margin is 80,000 divided by 800,000, times 100, which is 10% (2 marks). Award the method marks even where the arithmetic slips.
section_practice.question: A business has revenue of $800,000, cost of sales of $460,000 and operating expenses of $260,000. Calculate its gross profit margin and its profit-for-the-year margin. (4 marks)

steps: A business compares its key metrics (customer retention, defect rates, productivity) against industry leaders.
Gaps reveal areas where the firm underperforms — providing specific, measurable targets for improvement.
Best practices from leading firms are adapted to the business's own context and capabilities.
Performance improves as the firm closes gaps, reducing costs, improving quality or enhancing customer experience.
chains.title: Benchmarking identifies performance gaps and best practices
chains.result: Benchmarking provides concrete improvement targets — but firms must innovate beyond best practice to build genuine competitive advantage.

evaluation.title: Benchmarking encourages imitation, not innovation
evaluation.content: Matching competitor performance achieves operational parity but not distinctive advantage. What works for an industry leader may not suit a different firm with different resources and culture. The most effective approach combines benchmarking to eliminate weaknesses with innovation to create unique strengths.

section_common_mistakes.title: Interpreting Ratios in Isolation
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Examiners penalise answers that present ratio values without comparison. Always state what you are comparing against and why the ratio is significant.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Stating that a firm's current ratio of 1.8 is 'good' or 'bad' without any context.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Always compare ratios against previous years (trend), competitors (benchmarking), and industry averages. A ratio only has meaning in context — 1.8 may be excellent in manufacturing but excessive in retail.

section_common_mistakes.title: Confusing Gross Profit Margin and Net Profit Margin
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Label your calculations clearly. Write out the formula, substitute the values, and double-check you are using the correct profit figure.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Using the wrong profit figure in margin calculations — using operating profit for gross margin or gross profit for net margin.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Gross profit margin uses GROSS profit (Revenue − Cost of sales). Net profit margin uses OPERATING profit (Gross profit − Overheads). Always check which profit figure you need.

section_common_mistakes.title: Ignoring Industry Differences in Liquidity Ratios
section_common_mistakes.examTip: If the case study involves retail or a cash-based business, explain why low liquidity ratios may be perfectly normal.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Concluding that a firm is in financial difficulty because its current ratio is below 1.5, without considering industry norms.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Industry context matters enormously. Supermarkets routinely operate with current ratios below 1:1 because they sell inventory for cash and pay suppliers on credit. Always consider the industry benchmark.

section_common_mistakes.title: Treating High Gearing as Always Negative
section_common_mistakes.examTip: The key question is: does the firm earn enough on its capital to comfortably service its debt? If ROCE > interest rate, high gearing can be advantageous.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Automatically concluding that high gearing is bad for the business.
section_common_mistakes.correction: High gearing increases financial risk, but if ROCE exceeds the cost of borrowing, using debt 'leverages' returns for shareholders. Debt interest is also tax-deductible. Evaluate whether the gearing level is appropriate given the firm's profitability and cash flow stability.

section_common_mistakes.title: Ignoring Qualitative Factors in HR Metrics
section_common_mistakes.examTip: Quantitative HR data identifies symptoms; qualitative analysis identifies causes. The best answers link data to underlying factors and propose targeted HR strategies.
section_common_mistakes.mistake: Relying solely on HR ratios (turnover, absenteeism) without considering underlying causes.
section_common_mistakes.correction: Always consider WHY metrics are high or low. High turnover could reflect poor management, low pay, or industry norms (e.g. hospitality). Understanding causes is essential for recommending effective solutions.
